title: If only it were my field
translation: Someone who's an expert in one field goes along to a gathering in another and says, "Ah, if only this were my field! I wouldn't be sitting on the sidelines like this." People say it all the time, and think it too, but it strikes me as very bad manners. If you envy people in a field you don't know, just say, "I'm so jealous. Why didn't I ever learn this?"

Showing off what you know to beat other people is like an animal lowering its horns or baring its teeth. What makes a person good is not bragging about their strengths and not competing with anyone. Being better than other people at something is a serious fault in itself. Maybe it's your rank, maybe your talent, maybe your famous ancestors. If you think it puts you above other people, there's a lot wrong inside you, even if you never say it out loud. Be careful, and forget about it. When you look like a fool, get run down by other people or bring trouble on yourself, it's this pride, and nothing else.
People who have really mastered a field see their own shortcomings clearly. So they're never satisfied, and they never brag about anything.

literal: A person engaged in one way, attending a gathering of a different way, says, 'Ah, if it were my way, I would not be watching from outside like this', and thinks so in his heart too: this is common, but it seems very bad.
If one feels envious of a way one does not know, one should just say, 'Oh, how enviable; why did I not learn it?'
To bring out one's knowledge and compete with people is the same kind of thing as a horned creature tilting its horns and a fanged creature baring its fangs.
As a person, one counts it a virtue not to boast of one's good points and not to compete with others.
To have something in which one surpasses others is a great fault.

Whether in loftiness of rank, excellence in learning and arts, or the honour of one's ancestors, a person who thinks he surpasses others, even if he does not put it into words, has many faults in his heart.
One should be careful and forget this.
That one looks foolish, is run down by people, and invites misfortune: it is only this pride.
A person who has truly excelled in one way clearly knows his own faults himself, so his aim is never satisfied, and in the end he never boasts of anything.

notes.text: あらぬ{道|みち}: 'a way that is not (his)', another art. {席|むしろ}: 'mat', and so a gathering or session. The reading is the edition's.
ましかば: 'if it were', contrary to fact. He is not in that field. じものを: 'I would not…, and yet'.
…てありなむ: 'it would be fine to just…'. The same advice formula comes back in section 168.
'Not to boast of one's good points' is the wish of Confucius's student Yan Hui in the Analects (see section 129). Not competing is the subject of section 130, and an important idea in the Laozi.
{失|しつ}: a fault, a failing. A strong claim. The next sentences give the reason: the advantage brings pride with it.
{若干|そこばく}: 'many, a great deal' (the edition's reading). Modern Japanese reads 若干 じゃっかん and uses it for 'a few, some', almost the opposite. {科|とが}: a fault, a sin.

notes.quote: をこにも見え、人にもいひけたれ
notes.text: をこ: 'a fool' (the edition glosses it {馬鹿|ばか}). いひけたれ: 'to be talked down', from いひけつ.
{慢心|まんしん}: pride, conceit. 慢 is one of the defilements of the mind in Buddhist teaching. The word is still used today.
{志|こころざし}: aim, ambition. The master is never satisfied because he sees what he has not yet reached.
